findings.where: Hero heading, 'MARK · M · MOSELEY' over 'INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: Mark's name and his job title use the same face, size, weight, colour and tracking. Because the title line is longer, it runs much wider than the name and takes over the first screen. The interpunct between 'Infrastructure' and 'Advisor' makes the title look like more parts of the name rather than a role.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank visitor scanning the first screen. The brief says the man himself is the brand, but here his name gets less visual weight than a generic job description, and the eye goes first to 'INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR'.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the headline 'THE WORLD'S BEST PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP LAW' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: Article titles are set in Cinzel, which has capitals only, so a normal-length post title becomes a three-line block of all caps. Every word is the same height, so the title is slow to read. Longer titles, like the 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge' lecture shown below it, will turn into four or five lines of capitals.
findings.who_objects: A reader on an article page, which is in Read mode. All-caps titles lose word shapes and are harder to scan. Angélique, who will add posts with Mark's real, long titles and cannot shorten them to suit the face, would also object.

findings.where: Motion sketch panel, 'cubic-bezier(0.5, 0, 0.2, 1)' and 'docs/research/animation-length.md' in the running text (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: These phrases are in an unstyled default monospace. It looks larger and heavier than the Alegreya Sans around it, so it breaks the line spacing and stands out as a third face that belongs to no part of the type pair.
findings.who_objects: Mark or the founder reading the tile as the look of the site. The fallback mono looks like a mistake inside a carefully paired Cinzel and Alegreya system.

findings.where: Article page specimen on phone, the meta line 'MMM INFRA BLOG NO. 8 · 18 SEPTEMBER 2024'
findings.fault: The date breaks across lines, leaving the year '2024' alone on the second line.
findings.who_objects: A phone reader. A split date reads awkwardly and the stranded year looks like a separate item.
